{
  "story": "# UK MPs Deny Commons Vote Means Animals Not Recognised as Sentient Beings

MPs have been forced to deny that a Commons vote last week means animals are not recognised in the UK as sentient life forms, after a defeated amendment to the European Union (Withdrawal) Bill sparked widespread public outrage and accusations of governmental indifference to animal welfare.

The controversy erupted after an amendment to transfer the EU protocol on animal sentience into UK law was defeated by 313 votes to 295 on 15 November. The amendment, proposed by Green Party co-leader Caroline Lucas among others, had sought to specifically incorporate Article 13 of Title II of the Lisbon Treaty into UK law — a provision that explicitly recognises animals as sentient beings capable of feeling pain and emotion.

Since then, a fierce row has developed over what the vote actually meant in practice, with MPs from across the political spectrum scrambling to clarify their position as public anger mounted.

Describing some of the reporting on the vote as "weird and dishonest", Conservative MP Zac Goldsmith tweeted a clarification that the vote had been about the correct legal procedure for ensuring animal welfare standards — not on the principle of whether animals are sentient. Fellow Conservative Rachel Maclean, MP for Redditch, posted a video to try and explain the confusion caused by what she described as "fake news", stating that "this government, and in fact all governments, are deeply committed to continuing to protect animals as sentient beings. That law is already written into our own law."

The issue was raised at the highest levels of government when Prime Minister Theresa May addressed the matter at Wednesday's Prime Minister's Questions, declaring: "We recognise and respect that animals are sentient beings, and should be treated accordingly."

Meanwhile, Conservative MP Hugo Swire republished on social media a letter he had received from Michael Gove, the Environment Secretary, on the issue, adding: "I do not believe that any MP thinks that animals do not have feelings or emotions."

Despite these reassurances from government figures, the vote has triggered significant protests from animal rights groups, including multiple online petitions aimed at the House of Lords, UK Parliament, and Gove himself. Public figures including television presenter Sue Perkins have voiced strong criticism of MPs over the issue, amplifying the sense of public dismay.

The veterinary profession also weighed in with concern. Gudrun Ravetz, senior vice-president of the British Veterinary Association, said: "It is extremely concerning that a marginal majority of MPs have voted down this seminal clause. This action undermines the government's previous promises that the UK will continue to be known for our high standards of animal health and welfare post-Brexit."

The debate has exposed a fundamental tension at the heart of the Brexit process: as the UK prepares to leave the European Union, questions are being raised about which protections enshrined in EU law will survive the transition and which may fall through the cracks. The amendment's supporters argue that without explicit incorporation into domestic legislation, the recognition of animal sentience could be lost as EU law ceases to apply in the UK.

During the debate on the amendment last Wednesday, Lucas pointed out that the origins of the clause began with the 1997 UK presidency of the EU and that from 1999 EU law had explicitly recognised that animals were sentient life forms — making it ironic that the UK might now abandon a principle it had helped to champion on the European stage.

However, not all MPs accepted that the vote represented a backward step. Henry Smith, Conservative MP for Crawley, pointed out that EU law still allowed many practices across Europe that animal rights groups oppose, suggesting that membership of the EU had never been a guarantee of robust animal welfare standards.

The government's position appears to be that animal sentience is already recognised in existing UK legislation and that the defeated amendment was simply the wrong legal mechanism for addressing the issue. Ministers have indicated that they intend to bring forward separate provisions to ensure animal welfare standards are maintained after Brexit.

But for many campaigners and members of the public, the explanation rings hollow. The sight of a majority of MPs voting against an amendment that explicitly recognised animal sentience has proved deeply troubling, regardless of the technical legal arguments about procedure. The episode has become a lightning rod for broader anxieties about the potential erosion of rights and protections as the UK charts its course outside the European Union.

As the Withdrawal Bill continues its passage through Parliament, the government will likely face continued pressure to provide concrete legislative guarantees on animal sentience — and to demonstrate that Brexit will not come at the cost of the welfare standards that the UK once helped to establish at the European level."
}
```
